8827-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
This volume holds the preface and introductions to R. F. Weymouth's New Testament in Modern Speech, in its third edition of 1913. The files were keyed for the Online Bible from the Kregal reprint of the Ernest Hampden-Cook edition, first published in 1909 by J. Clarke of London, with proofreading by Earl Melton. Footnote markers, page-break indicators, asterisks for emphasis, and angle brackets for bold Old Testament quotations are left in the text, as the editors planned to add Weymouth's footnotes.

Weymouth aimed to render the Greek in the plain, living English of his day, rather than in King James cadence. That ordinary readers could follow Paul and the evangelists without a commentary. The preface and introductions explain his principles, his text, and his choices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bois-le-duc:
Bois-le-Duc, a Dutch diocese in Brabant suffragan to Utrecht, was raised to a see in 1561 to check the spread of Protestantism. Its city, founded in 1184, had belonged to Liege. Pius IV made it suffragan to Mechlin, and its first bishop was the theologian Francis Sonnius, who served from 1562 to 1569.

War and siege battered his successors, and in 1629 the city fell to Prince Frederick Henry. Bishop Ophorius left in solemn procession, carrying a famed statue of the Virgin to Brussels. Under Westphalia in 1648 the territory passed to the States-General, Catholic worship was banned by law, and priests ministered in secret. The diocese stayed a mission under vicars apostolic until 1853.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evariste-regi:
Evariste Regis Huc was a French Lazarist missionary and traveler, born at Caylus in 1813 and dead at Paris in 1860. He joined the Congregation of the Mission in 1836, and reached China in 1839, and reached the new Vicariate of Tartary-Mongolia, where he lived until 1844. That year his bishop ordered him and his fellow missionary Joseph Gabet to explore the mission lands and study the nomadic Mongol tribes they were to convert.

On 3 August 1844 the two men set out from the Valley of the Black Waters, some three hundred miles north of Peking, with a young lama as sole companion. After eighteen months through Dolon-nor, the Ordo country, Ala-shan, Si-ning, and the Kun-Bum monastery, they reached Lhasa, capital of Tibet, on 29 January 1846. The Chinese commissioner expelled them within a month, and they reached Canton that September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fronton-du-du:
Fronton du Duc, a French Jesuit born at Bordeaux in 1558, gave the Church its great early edition of Saint John Chrysostom. He first taught in Jesuit colleges and wrote a tragic play on the Maid of Orléans, acted in 1581. Later he joined the theological battles of his day, answering the Huguenot Du Plessis-Mornay on the Eucharist in a sharp inventory of faults.

Chosen to revise the Greek Fathers from the royal library, du Duc published Chrysostom at Paris between 1609 and 1624, with a two-volume Library of the Ancient Fathers as companion. As librarian of the Collège de Clermont from 1604, he rebuilt a library scattered in exile. He also began revising the Greek Bible text, a task he left unfinished at his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-astruc:
Jean Astruc, born at Sauves in 1684 and dead in Paris in 1766, was a French physician whose side work changed Bible study. Son of a converted Protestant minister, he taught medicine at Montpellier and joined the Paris medical faculty. His medical books are now forgotten.

Astruc's lasting book, printed without his name, argued that Moses drew on older written memoirs when composing Genesis, and offered notes to back or clarify that guess. He did not mean to deny that Moses authored Genesis, yet his idea opened a new era of inquiry. Later critics built whole theories of the Bible's sources on the path his conjectures first marked out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-belain:
Pierre Belain, sieur d'Esnambuc, founded France's Antilles colonies and governed them first, born at Allouville near Yvetot in 1565. Sailing from Dieppe in 1625 on a four-gun brigantine with thirty-five men, he seized St. Christopher. Returning to France, he persuaded Richelieu to form the Company of the American Islands in October 1626, with authority over St. Christopher and Barbados.

For ten years he bent all his energies to spreading French influence through the islands, recruiting colonists across Lower Normandy, chiefly around Dieppe, Honfleur, and Le Havre. Flourishing settlements rose in Guadeloupe, Dominica, Les Saintes, and Marie-Galante. In September 1635 he landed 150 determined men at Martinique and built St. Pierre the next year. He died at St. Christopher in December 1636, leaving his nephews the overseas realm he had begun. Richelieu mourned a great servant lost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rolduc:
Rolduc is an abbey in southeastern Limburg in the Netherlands, founded as an Augustinian house in 1104. Its founder, the Venerable Ailbertus, a priest and son of a Flemish nobleman, was guided by a vision to Count Adelbert's domain. The count handed over the abbey and church property in 1108. Ailbertus served as first abbot until 1111, founded Clairfontaine in France, and died at Sechtem in 1122.

Thirty-eight abbots followed him, the last being Peter Joseph Chaineux, who served until 1800. The abbey grew rich, became the burial place of the Dukes of Limburg, and owned a famous 1230 catalogue listing 140 theological and 86 other works. Its crypt was blessed in 1106, and its church, dedicated to the Virgin and St Gabriel, was completed in 1209. The church holds a reputed relic of the Holy Cross and the body of St Daphne from the Roman catacombs. Rolduc became a seminary in 1831 and an academy in 1841.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-brieuc:
Saint-Brieuc is a diocese comprising the Cotes du Nord department. The Concordat of 1802 restored it under Tours, and in 1850 it passed under Rennes. It also took most of Treguier, part of old St Malo, Dol, and Quimper, and parishes of Vannes. In 1852 its bishops added the ancient See of Treguier to their title.

The ancient diocese sprang from an Irish saint, Briocus, who died early in the sixth century. He founded a monastery for St Stephen that bore his name and gave rise to the town. An inscription on his tomb at Angers calls him the first Bishop of Saint-Brieuc. Trustworthy documents prove that King Nomenoe about the mid-ninth century made the monastery a bishopric's seat. Among its bishops were St Guillaume Pinchon, 1220 to 1234. Jean du Tillet and Denis de La Barde follow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-brieuc:
St. Brieuc, or Briocus, Brioc, or Bru, was a Celtic saint of Brittany, educated in Ireland and then under St. Germanus, said to be the famous St. Germanus of Auxerre. This entry follows a life whose early years must be received with caution. Ussher asserts Irish birth for him, but he almost certainly returned to France early in 431, bringing St. Iltud. Even before ordination, Brieuc worked miracles chronicled in his Acts.

After a short period with his parents, his missionary career began. In 480 he settled in Armorica, founding a monastery at Landebaeron. Thence he went to Upper Brittany, where he established an oratory at the place known as St. Brieuc-des-Vaux, between St. Malo and Land Triguier, and was named its first bishop. The Acts cite numerous miracles, especially for the poor and the sick, and the entry presents a bishop of Brittany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-william-bi:
William of St-Brieuc, bishop in Brittany, is known for virtues and miracles rather than deeds. Born in the parish of St Alban in Brittany between 1178 and 1184 to Oliver Pinchon and Jane Fortin, he was elected bishop in the early 1220s. The Acts of the Saints tell only of his virtues and miracles, giving no details of his life.

He counted himself father of the poor and afflicted of his diocese, defended clerical rights, and angered the powerful enough to be banished. He lived for a time in the diocese of Poitiers, helping its sick bishop, and returned in 1230. He began building a cathedral but died before finishing it. Canonised on 15 April 1247 by Innocent IV, his relics were burned in the French Revolution. His feast falls on 29 July.

podcast-dannyjones-eCWZGZAJJUc:
Dalia Burgoin joins Danny Jones to talk about her child, whom she says is telepathic, and how others can wake the same gift. The episode title calls her the mother of a telepathic child. Her claims go far past what science accepts.

Burgoin tells how she first saw signs of the gift and how her child sends thoughts without words. She shares the steps she says any person can use to open the same skill. Jones asks gentle but firm questions about proof. Listeners get a tender, strange talk on a mother's claim. The library holds it as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-YebZyAzLZuc:
Physicist Michio Kaku tells Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, about the shift in the UFO phenomenon. Kaku, a famous explainer of cosmic physics, notes how the subject moved from late-night radio to Senate hearings and Navy videos. His own view has moved with the evidence.

He explains what the new data would mean if the craft are real, in terms of physics and energy no human tech can match. Rogan asks what would convince the last doubters. The segment is a short, clear sample of a mainstream scientist treating an old fringe subject with new respect.
podcast-joerogan-acbD70wFTuc:
Rock legend John Mellencamp talks songs and small towns with Joe Rogan in episode 2438. Mellencamp's hits like Jack and Diane and Small Town defined heartland rock in the 1980s. Now also a painter, he speaks in his trademark blunt, unfiltered style.

Mellencamp looks back on fame, the music business, and the Indiana roots he never left. He shares his dim view of modern culture and phone-driven life. Rogan draws out stories from the long road of tours and records. Music fans and the nostalgic get the rocker as he is: stubborn, funny, and plain-spoken.
podcast-tuckercarlson-Vv9Bh6Pu3uc:
Tucker Carlson speaks alone in a monologue episode of his podcast about faith and power in the age of Donald Trump. He argues that support for Trump has taken on the shape of a new religion. He also charges that critics mock Jesus Christ and treat Christian belief with open scorn.

Carlson ties the mood of the country to a deeper shift in faith, politics, and shared culture. Listeners hear his case in his own words, with no guest to push back or agree. The episode gives his audience a clear view of how he frames loyalty, belief, and the fights now splitting American public life.
poems-teachers-ask-for-selected-by-reade:
Readers of Normal Instructor-Primary Plans, a magazine for elementary teachers, voted with their requests to build this anthology. Which prints the poems most frequently asked for on the magazine's request page. No professor edited the canon here; classroom need did. A teacher who had seen a poem work with real children wrote in for it, and the most wanted pieces were gathered between covers.

The index opens with Leigh Hunt's Abou Ben Adhem and runs through Drake's American Flag. Whittier's Barbara Frietchie and Barefoot Boy, Longfellow's Arrow and the Song, and Thayer's Casey at the Bat. Nature lyrics, moral tales in verse, and patriotic recitations dominate, all tested by use. As a record of taste, the book is invaluable: this is what American schoolrooms around the turn of the century actually memorized, recited, and loved.
